content:
The image shows a corn leaf with a distinct elongated lesion running along the midrib/vein area. Key features:

- **Location**: Along the midrib/vein of a corn leaf
- **Color**: Deep reddish-brown to dark red lesion with a pale/white center stripe
- **Pattern**: Elongated, narrow lesion confined to the midrib region
- **Texture**: Small black fungal structures (sporangia/fruiting bodies) embedded within the lesion at regular intervals
- **Surrounding tissue**: Green leaf with some yellowing/chlorotic flecking around the lesion
- **The black dots** are discrete, round, embedded structures — consistent with fungal sporangia

The pattern of dark reddish-brown lesions along the midrib with embedded black sporangial clusters at regular intervals is highly characteristic of **Physoderma Brown Spot**. Physoderma maydis infects corn through node tissue and midrib, producing reddish-brown to purple-brown lesions on the midrib with dark brown to black sporangia embedded in the tissue. The alternating pattern of dark spots along the reddish midrib lesion is the textbook signature of this disease.

This is distinct from Tar Spot (which produces discrete, raised black stromata scattered across the blade), Purple Leaf Sheath (which affects the sheath, not midrib), or Physoderma Stalk Rot (which affects the stalk node).
